limitations: SWD reads span 103-180 ms and are not atomic; tick_after minus feedback_ms cannot certify or reject the firmware 30 ms freshness condition.
Direction checks use RUNNING samples and ignore motor targets within 0.15 rad/s of zero; phase-transition and STOP tails are excluded.
One backward transition has manual_state=0 with earlier-read enabled=1; subsequent samples consistently show disabled. This is compatible with non-atomic transition sampling.
Three motor sequence counters need not be identical because CAN replies are asynchronous; each must progress.
Wheel-derived body speeds are estimates with the wheels raised, not independently measured chassis motion or ground-test stability.
No precise tracking RMSE or stop latency is inferred from these asynchronous reads. This log does not test sender-loss timeout.
Final disabled feedback is newer than each action RUNNING interval; its later age while disabled is expected without periodic MIT commands.

new_motor_disabled_feedback.meaning: These are CAN feedback receive timestamps for state=0 and quiet wheels, not exact physical stopping times.

limitations: All observation intervals use device xTickCount, with the frozen command received_ms as zero unless stated otherwise.
SWD field reads are sequential. Transition bounds use the previous contrary sample start through the first matching sample end, not an assumed atomic sampling time.

The first disarmed sample combines pending_disable=1 read earlier with new motor state=0 read later. The following sample confirms pending_disable=0; this is compatible with a transition during the read.
Inter-command receive gap is observable; exact SIGSTOP/SIGCONT times are not recorded here.
Resumed expired timed command produces valid zero-speed preparation/ready frames before invalid stop frames. Brief zero-speed re-enabling is expected.
Wheel feedback with wheels raised does not establish ground-motion stopping distance or chassis stability.
The earlier usb_timeout_summary.json is retained as an inconclusive observation window and is not overwritten.

field_optimization_live_performance.scope: Sequential fresh 30-second live windows on current negative/tabletop SEARCH scene

assessment.interpretation: The optimized field path materially improves recognition and delivered video throughput. It does not improve every latency metric: encode/publish age tails, JPEG encoding time and worst receive intervals increase, and the stream queue replaces 4 frames. This is a modest stream-side tail regression rather than an observed transport/camera failure; it does not negate the measured throughput improvement.
assessment.practical_significance: Retain the optimization on this evidence while reporting the tail tradeoff. PC receive p95 remains about 47 ms, worst gap rises from 78 to 94 ms, and PC delivery rises from 50.4667 to 69.5667 fps. Do not describe the new stream as uniformly lower-latency or lossless for every recognition frame.
assessment.possible_contributors_not_proven: The optimized window has higher total JPEG traffic, about 4.2% larger average JPEGs, and slightly more simultaneous viewers. These differences can contribute to stream/CPU/network tail load, but this sequential live pair does not isolate a cause.

limitations: Both live windows contain only SEARCH/none results: 0 valid or committed fields among 1513 baseline and 2146 optimized messages. This pair measures no-candidate scene throughput, not positive-field tracking accuracy or full-scene accuracy equivalence.

Baseline and optimized were sequential live windows, not identical fixed-image replay. Camera contents/noise/exposure and load can vary; source reports do not contain frame-by-frame input equivalence or configuration hashes.

The task requires unchanged source/processing resolution, thresholds and image quality. These six reports do not independently prove those settings; implementation review and separate matched-input regression evidence establish that claim.
ROS status FPS values are window counters; inference and composition latency status values are smoothed EMA samples. Their means are not independent per-frame latency percentiles.
The ROS and HTTP measurements each last 30 seconds but start at different times. Their rates/counts cannot be subtracted as an exact count of lost frames.
HTTP sequence continuity proves continuity of emitted JPEGs observed by each client. Frames replaced or skipped before JPEG publication do not create HTTP sequence gaps.
Four stream queue replacements are observed in the optimized ROS status window versus zero baseline. This counter alone cannot explain the entire recognition-to-video rate difference.
Server frame-age headers end at encode/publish, exclude network/client display time and are not end-to-end motion-to-photon latency.
PC timestamps are visibly quantized (including zero receive intervals); its maximum gap is a single observed sample, not a stable worst-case guarantee.
Camera reopen and probe error checks are limited to these reports and sample windows; they are not an exhaustive journal/kernel fault audit.
